column1: # Korean rewrite rules (W) over kir nodes. They edit nodes and features, never text. Phases run disc then ko;
# inside a phase rules run in id order, each at most once per site. Cases: rules.cases.tsv (fix and keep).
#   pattern    node matchers [Kind lemma|lemma {feat=v|w,feat!=v}]:name, `?` optional, `...` gap inside the
#              clause, `^` clause start (line start or after 「 。 ！ ？), `$` clause end
#   condition  `-` or atoms joined by &: x.feat=v|w, x.feat!=v, x.clauselen<=n, x.prev.feat=v, x.next.feat=v,
#              utt.level=v, utt.narration, utt.quote; `!` negates an atom
#   action     `;`-joined: set x.feat=v | copy x.feat=y.feat | del x | replace x [Kind lemma {feats}] |

column7: -고 있다 is the progressive aspect of the verb (D §2.1): rules and G see one predicate
K1: no comma after a line-initial conjunction or interjection (하지만, 문제도 → 하지만 문제도)
K1: no comma after a connective clause of one or two words (그렇게 생각해서, → 그렇게 생각해서)
a comma the source does not have
K1: no comma after a short topic (나는, → 나는)
로부터 → 에서 / 에게서 (G chooses by animacy; 34× overuse)
의-chains: A의 B의 C → A B의 C when A is not a person
casual speech says 너, not 당신 (6.2 vs 2.0 per 1,000 lines)
polite speech drops the addressee pronoun
casual speech says 걔 for 彼女 (그녀 is written style)
K5: state verbs do not take -고 있다 in the present (알고 있어 → 알아)
